title: Fix the worktree test that fails its own cleanup
description:
TestManagerIntegrateRefusesNonFastForwardAndKeepsHarnessCommit fails intermittently in CI during teardown, not assertion: 'TempDir RemoveAll cleanup: unlinkat .../repository/.git: directory not empty'. Its checks pass; Go's t.TempDir cleanup then races something still holding or repopulating the repository directory, most likely a git worktree registration or a background git process that has not exited.

Observed on pull request 13 (run 31992104553) for yoyodyne-ifd.21, where it blocked the merge. The same commit passed the harness's own make test, make race and make vet, so this reproduces in CI and not locally.

P0 because build is a required status check on a protected main: a test that fails intermittently in teardown blocks every publication, and the harness cannot merge past it. It also teaches the wrong lesson -- a red required check that is usually spurious is one people stop reading.
design:
Make the test responsible for what it created rather than leaving it to TempDir. A worktree the test registered should be removed by the test before cleanup runs, and any git invocation it started should be waited for, so the directory is genuinely idle when Go tries to delete it.

Prefer fixing the leak to retrying the deletion. A cleanup that retries until the directory goes quiet hides whichever handle is still open, and that handle is the interesting thing: if a git process outlives the call that started it, the harness has the same problem outside tests.

Check the sibling tests in internal/gitworktree for the same shape before assuming this one is unique. The failure is timing-dependent, so the one that fails is not necessarily the only one that can.
acceptance_criteria: The test cleans up the worktrees and processes it creates so TempDir removal has nothing to race; it passes repeatedly under CI conditions, including with -count high enough to expose the race; no cleanup step retries deletion to paper over a held handle; sibling tests with the same pattern are corrected too.
notes:

title: Queue the merge with --auto so required checks are waited for
description:
Publishing merges the moment the reviewer approves, but a protected branch will not accept a merge until its required checks have passed. CI takes about forty seconds and the harness asks within seconds of approving, so the merge is refused on essentially every run.

Observed on the first published run, run-ab96b7a966d3b718dc9287d9f5846725 for yoyodyne-ifd.20.1. The run succeeded, the reviewer approved, the work integrated locally and pull request 5 opened, and the merge was refused: 'the base branch's protection rules are not satisfied (BLOCKED) ... the base branch policy prohibits the merge.' GitHub's own message names the remedy: add --auto to have the pull request merged once the requirements are met.

Nothing is lost when this happens -- the outcome is reported as 'the change is integrated locally; the pull request still needs to be reconciled by hand' -- but it leaves an open pull request and an unpushed local branch after every run, which is precisely the manual reconciliation that publishing exists to remove.
design:
Ask GitHub to merge when the requirements are met rather than asking it to merge now. gh pr merge --auto queues the merge and lets the forge complete it once required checks pass, which is what a protected branch is asking for.

Auto-merge is a repository setting, so it can be unavailable. Detect that and say so plainly rather than failing obscurely: a repository with auto-merge disabled and required checks configured cannot be published to this way, and the operator should be told which setting to change.

Do not reach for --admin. Merging with administrator privileges bypasses the very checks the protection expresses, and a harness that routinely overrides branch protection has removed the gate rather than satisfied it.

The confirmation loop needs rethinking alongside this. It currently asks three times over seven seconds whether the merge landed, which suited an immediate merge and cannot suit a queued one. A queued merge completes minutes later, so the run should record the pull request as queued and finish, rather than waiting for something that will not happen while it watches. What reconciliation does about a queued merge that later fails is the open question worth answering here.
acceptance_criteria: A merge into a protected branch with required checks succeeds without manual reconciliation; the harness queues the merge rather than demanding it immediately; a repository that cannot auto-merge is reported with the setting that needs changing rather than a generic refusal; administrator override is never used to bypass protection; a run whose merge is queued finishes and reports the pull request as queued rather than blocking on a confirmation that cannot arrive; reconciliation defines what happens to a queued merge that later fails.
notes:
Found 2026-08-16 on the first run after enabling branch protection and approvals.publishing. P0 because it affects every published run and reintroduces the manual step publishing was meant to remove.

title: Do not discard a completed run over provider output after the terminal result
description:
internal/backend/claudecode/parser.go rejects any line arriving after the provider's terminal result envelope: ParseLine returns 'provider event received after terminal result' as a fatal error. The Claude Code CLI does emit trailing events after its result, so a run whose developer finished successfully is thrown away.

Observed on run-44a559a57d3710e6cd99125efd29ee2d for yoyodyne-ifd.12. The developer completed and emitted its final summary at sequence 586; the run then failed with that parse error, discarding 975 insertions of finished work that never reached checks or review. The error repeated three times in the output, so more than one trailing event arrived.

This is a reliability defect affecting every run, not a problem specific to that work item, which is why it is P0: any run can complete its work and then be discarded for output the provider legitimately emits. It also interacts with yoyodyne-ifd.12, since a rate-limit notice is one of the things plausibly arriving late.
design:
A terminal result means the run's outcome is decided; it does not mean the provider stops writing. Record events that arrive after it rather than failing on them, and keep the already-decided result. Guard the actual invariant, which is that a second terminal result must not silently replace the first, rather than treating all trailing output as corruption.

Preserve what the trailing events carry instead of discarding it. They are exactly where a late rate-limit notice would appear, and yoyodyne-ifd.12 needs that payload. Do not let a post-terminal event mutate the recorded result, session identifier, resolved model, usage, or cost, since those belong to the terminal envelope; append them to the event stream so they remain diagnosable.
acceptance_criteria: A provider event arriving after the terminal result no longer fails the run; the terminal result, session identifier, resolved model, usage, and cost are unchanged by anything arriving after it; trailing events appear in the recorded event stream; a second terminal result is still rejected rather than replacing the first; a test replays a stream with events after the result and asserts the run succeeds with the original outcome intact.

title: Rewrite the README to lead with value and match what exists
description:
The README has grown by accretion: each landed item patched its own section, so the file now reads as a pile of mechanics in landing order -- quick start, run internals, usage limits, recovery, then the conversation almost as an afterthought. The operator wants it to reasonably reflect the current state and lead with the value.

The value, as the product now actually works: an operator states intent in a conversation with a product manager that reads the product's own brief and goals, approves proposed work in batches, and watches the harness implement it in an isolated worktree, check it deterministically, review it independently, repair it when the reviewer objects, and publish it through a pull request that merges itself when CI passes -- with every gate enforced by the harness rather than by convention. The conversation is the product; yoyo run and yoyo reconcile are administrative entry points, which the design document has said for some time while the README still leads with them.

Amended by the operator, 2026-08-17: the README must also let someone else set this up and use it on their own project. Today it cannot -- the quick start assumes an initialized Yoyodyne checkout, and nowhere says how to obtain the binary, prepare a fresh repository, or adopt the harness in a project that is not Yoyodyne itself.
design:
Lead with what an operator gets, then how to get started, then how it works. A reasonable shape: what Yoyodyne does for you in a few sentences with the conversation front and center; the quick start; the conversation as the primary interface including proposals, batch decisions, /status, /work, /show, /diff, /refresh and freshness; how work flows once approved -- worktree, checks, independent review, repair loop, publication and auto-merge; configuration with the explicit file and personas; operations and recovery, including usage limits and reconcile; then pointers to the design document and configuration guide.

The discipline matters more than the structure: this repository has already shipped a README that asserted something false about the product, it surfaced as the product manager confidently reporting it to the operator as fact, and ifd.11 exists because of it. The product manager reads this file as evidence, so every sentence must be true of the current build -- lead with value, never ahead of reality. Where a capability is real but bounded (one run at a time, no scheduler, no development manager yet), say the bound in the same breath rather than leaving the reader to infer more than exists.

title: Make proposals decidable in batches, and let the operator read items and diffs in-chat
description:
Proposals are decided one at a time: each is printed and the operator answers y or yes serially, which will grate the first time the product manager proposes five things at once. And two things the operator regularly wants mid-conversation still require leaving it: reading a work item in full (bd show) and seeing what a run actually changed (GitHub or git).

Three parts. First, render proposals as visually distinct numbered cards, using the theme. Second, batch decisions: approve 1,3 and decline 2 <reason> act on several at once, with the existing per-item semantics unchanged underneath -- approval is still recorded before creation, a decline still keeps its reason, an unanswered proposal is still named when the conversation ends. Third, /show <id> prints a work item in full, and /diff [id] shows what the conversation's running or last-finished run changed, from the durable run record.
design:
Batching changes the prompt, not the contract: the fail-closed rule from ifd.4.5 holds exactly -- nothing is created without an explicit approval naming it, an ambiguous answer declines, and each decision is recorded individually. A batch approval is several approvals, not a new kind.

/show reads through the same tracker capability the product manager already has, so what the operator sees is what the agent could see. /diff reads the durable run state and the recorded change summary rather than shelling out to git against a worktree that may already be gone; a run whose worktree was cleaned up still has its diff stat and pull request to point at.

Cards are presentation: the theme's discipline applies, and the recorded proposal payload is untouched.
acceptance_criteria: Multiple proposals render as numbered cards and can be approved and declined in one answer, with each decision recorded exactly as the serial flow records it today; nothing is created without an explicit approval naming the item; /show prints any work item in full from inside the conversation; /diff reports what the conversation's current or most recent run changed, including after cleanup; recorded payloads, the event stream, and --json are unchanged.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16. This is the acting half of the usability request: the things an operator does most -- deciding proposals, checking what something is, checking what a run did -- should not require leaving the conversation or a serial interrogation.

title: Tell the operator how fresh the conversation's picture is, and let them refresh it
description:
The sharpest conversational failure observed so far is staleness reported as fact: twice on 2026-08-16 the product manager confidently described the repository as it was when the conversation opened, not as it stood -- once insisting documentation still said yoyodyne after it had been renamed. The mechanism is documented (the briefing is gathered once and sent on the first turn only) and the README explains when to use --new, but the operator has to remember all of that. The conversation itself never says how old its picture is.

Three parts. First, on open and resume, say when the briefing was gathered and what has moved since: 'context gathered 2h ago; 14 commits and 3 tracker changes since'. Second, a /refresh command that re-reads the repository and tracker into the running conversation without discarding it, which --new cannot do. Third, render the product manager's markdown instead of printing it raw, and colour-code /status output with the states coloured consistently: running blue, blocked orange, done green, failed red.
design:
Freshness is a comparison, not a timestamp: the briefing already records when it was assembled, and the repository and tracker can say cheaply what has changed since -- commit count from git, tracker changes from the interactions log. Print it where the operator cannot miss it, on open and after resuming, and keep it to one line.

/refresh sends the delta into the conversation as evidence, the way harness activity notices already travel: it must not silently replace what the product manager believes, it tells it what changed and lets the next reply reconcile. State plainly in the transcript that a refresh happened. A conversation that was refreshed and one that was opened fresh should end up equally current but keep different histories, and that difference is the point of the command.

Markdown rendering is presentation only, in the console layer beside the existing theme: bold, headings, lists, and rules, degrading to plain text when output is not a terminal, never touching the recorded reply. Reuse the theme's colour discipline from ifd.28: colour is an addition, every distinction survives stripping, NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb are honoured.
acceptance_criteria: Opening or resuming a conversation states when its context was gathered and what has changed since; /refresh brings the running conversation current without discarding it and the transcript says it happened; the product manager's replies render markdown in a terminal and plain text elsewhere; /status output is aligned and colour-coded with the same state colours used elsewhere; the recorded conversation and --json output are unchanged by any of it.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: general request for the conversation to be easier to understand and more enjoyable. This item is the trust half: the operator should never have to wonder whether the product manager's picture is current.

title: Ship an explicit project configuration instead of inheriting hidden defaults
description:
A project configuration currently says almost nothing and inherits the rest. .yoyodyne/config.yaml carries thirteen meaningful lines and one extends: builtin:v1, while the five agents, their backends, model selectors, instance counts, and personas are supplied invisibly by a bundle inside the executable. The operator's judgement, 2026-08-16: this is difficult to reason about and more machinery than the problem needs.

The size argument for inheritance does not survive measurement. The fully expanded configuration is seventy-nine lines, and the five bundled personas are one hundred and seventy lines between them. That is roughly two hundred and fifty lines of things an operator might legitimately want to change, which is a file, not a burden.

What replaces it is a project that owns its configuration outright: every agent, selector, and persona written down where it can be read and edited, with nothing arriving from somewhere the reader cannot see.
design:
Generate rather than hand-write. yoyo init is already named in the design document's CLI surface and is the natural place: it writes a complete .yoyodyne/config.yaml with every agent stated explicitly, and copies the personas into .yoyodyne/personas/ so their text is editable in the project too. The embedded bundle survives as the template init writes from rather than as a runtime inheritance mechanism.

The cost of this is real and should be recorded rather than discovered: a project that owns its defaults stops receiving improvements to them. Better persona wording or a corrected model selector in a later Yoyodyne reaches a project only if someone re-runs init and merges the difference. Inheritance bought that and this trades it away deliberately, which is the right trade for a single-operator tool whose operator reads the file, and the wrong one for a fleet.

Keep the layering. The operator settled this on 2026-08-16: a portable configuration system is still wanted, just not yet, so extends survives as a capability while the explicit file becomes the shape a project is shipped with. Do not delete the inheritance code in internal/config or the rules tightened around it; this changes the default experience, not what the harness can express.

That means the deliverable is narrower than a rewrite. Nothing about resolution has to change. What changes is what init writes, what this repository's own configuration looks like, and what the documentation presents as the ordinary shape.

Whatever is chosen, this repository's own configuration should be migrated as part of the work, so the product is used the way it is shipped.
acceptance_criteria: yoyo init writes a complete project configuration with every agent, backend, model selector, instance count, and persona stated explicitly, and copies the persona files into the project; a project configured that way loads with no reference to a built-in bundle; extends still works for a project that uses it, and the inheritance code is retained rather than removed; this repository's own .yoyodyne/config.yaml is migrated to the explicit form; the documentation describes the explicit file as the shipped shape, and states plainly that a project owning its defaults no longer receives later improvements to them.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: 'the config file has everything commented out so that the defaults are used. I'm finding this difficult to reason about and probably a bit more complicated than we need. Replace all the defaults with explicit configurations in .yoyodyne. End users can just modify it as they see fit for their own projects.'

This reverses the direction of ifd.4.2, which introduced the bundle so a project could record only what was genuinely its own. That reasoning was about portability, and an explicit file is equally portable -- it travels with the project and needs no Yoyodyne checkout. What it gives up is shared improvement, not portability. 

Operator clarification, 2026-08-16: 'we will want those later. But at this stage of the project, I will be modifying agent properties regularly. I want those changes to be clear and obvious. That is to say, the design for a more portable agent configuration system remains a TODO.'

So this is a staging decision rather than an architectural reversal. Explicit configuration is what a project gets now, because the operator edits agent properties often and wants the effect of an edit obvious. Inheritance stays in the code and remains the answer for portability later, tracked as ifd.36. ifd.4.3 therefore stays relevant: the bundle continues to exist as the template init writes from.

title: Merge through the forge instead of pushing the target branch
description:
Publishing merges by pushing the integrated commit straight to the remote target branch and then waiting for the forge to report the pull request merged (internal/orchestrator/publish.go, 'push the integrated target branch', then awaitMerge). It never asks the forge to merge.

That works only on an unprotected branch. A repository that requires a pull request before merging -- which is the ordinary reason to open pull requests at all -- refuses the push, so the harness cannot complete the promotion it just earned. The operator wants main protected against direct pushes, and this is what stands in the way.

It also means the pull request is closed as a side effect of its commits appearing on the base, rather than merged deliberately. The forge's own record of who merged it, and by what method, is whatever it infers.
design:
Ask the forge to merge the pull request, and treat its answer as the outcome. The reviewer's approving verdict is still what authorizes it and the harness is still what acts, so the ownership rule is unchanged; only the mechanism moves from a push to a merge call.

Everything that gates integration today must still gate it: passing checks, an approving verdict, distinct developer and reviewer sessions, and a target that has not drifted. A forge merge is not an excuse to stop checking drift -- the remote can move between the check and the call, and the merge must fail rather than resolve a conflict the harness never saw.

Keep the local target branch authoritative, as ifd.29 decided. The local fast-forward still happens; what changes is that the remote arrives at the same commit through the forge rather than through a push. Decide what happens when the two disagree -- a forge that merged while the local branch did not advance is a state worth reporting rather than reconciling silently.

Choose the merge method deliberately and record it, because it decides what the history looks like: a merge commit, a squash, or a rebase produce different remote histories, and only one of them leaves the remote commit equal to the local one.

Report a refusal as what it is. A protected branch declining the merge because a required check has not run is not a harness failure, and the operator should be told which requirement was unmet.
acceptance_criteria: An approving verdict causes the harness to merge the pull request through the forge rather than by pushing the target branch; a protected branch that requires pull requests can be merged into successfully; checks, verdict, session independence, and target drift still gate the merge; the merge method is explicit and the resulting relationship between the local and remote target is defined; a forge refusal names the unmet requirement rather than being reported as a generic failure; a repository with no remote or with publishing disabled behaves exactly as it does today.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16, when asked how to sequence branch protection: fix the merge path first, then enable protection requiring pull requests, requiring the build check, and including administrators. Blocks that protection work.

title: Make provider integration a plugin contract users can extend
description:
Everything the harness knows about rate limits, retries, and when to try again is Claude Code's dialect, sitting in internal/backend/claudecode. The parser knows the rate_limit_event envelope, the field names status, resetsAt, rateLimitType, isUsingOverage, and overageStatus, that resetsAt is Unix seconds, that api_retry is the provider's own transient retry, and now that a rejection with no reset time means poll in thirty minutes. None of that is general, and all of it is load-bearing.

Codex is already a planned backend (yoyodyne-ifd.6), and the operator wants users to be able to reach further than that: to write a plugin for whatever harness or API they use, including an OpenAI-compatible one, without changing Yoyodyne.

The existing AgentBackend interface and its Capabilities call are the right instinct but the wrong altitude for this: they abstract starting and resuming a run, not the operational dialect of a provider -- how it says it is throttled, how it says it is exhausted, how to tell those apart, and when to come back.
design:
What the harness needs from a provider is a small set of answers, and the contract should be those answers rather than a way to reach in and parse. Given a provider event: is this an ordinary retry the provider is handling itself, a limit that will lift, or a refusal that will not; and if it will lift, when. The two hard cases are the ones already learned and should be named in the contract rather than rediscovered by each plugin: a limit that names no reset time is unknown rather than fatal and needs a default recheck interval, and a report that names a reset time in the past is malformed and must not be trusted.

Decide how a plugin is delivered, because Go makes this a real choice rather than a detail. Compile-time registration is simple and forces users to fork or vendor. A subprocess speaking a documented protocol keeps them independent and adds a boundary to defend, which matters because the thing on the other side is untrusted. A declarative adapter -- patterns and field mappings in configuration -- covers the common case of an API that differs only in spelling, and covers nothing else. The choice should be made explicitly with its trade stated, not arrived at.

Whatever is chosen, the plugin describes and never decides. It reports what a provider said; the harness decides whether to wait, how long, and against which budget, because those decisions are what the operator's usage_limit settings and the run's safety properties depend on. A plugin that could decide to keep waiting could spend an account.

Keep the capability model honest as it grows. Codex is already documented as not matching every Claude Code feature, and an unsupported role or policy combination fails validation before work is assigned; that must hold for a plugin nobody here has seen.
acceptance_criteria: Rate-limit, retry, and reset-time interpretation lives behind a documented provider contract rather than in the Claude Code adapter; the Claude Code behavior is one implementation of that contract with no special casing above it; a second provider can be added without changing harness code, and the delivery mechanism for a user-supplied one is documented with its trade-offs stated; a plugin reports what a provider said and never decides whether or how long to wait; the unknown-reset and past-reset cases are part of the contract rather than per-plugin behavior; capability validation refuses an unsupported role or policy combination for a plugin as it does for a built-in backend.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: 'these are all claude specific details. We'll want codex integration soon, so we need to abstract these things -- the pattern of the messages, how to determine when to check again, what to do when we can't determine when to check again. The goal there should be that there's a pluggable framework that end users of this product can use to extend and create a plugin for the harness (or api, eg openai's api standard) of their choice.'

Sequenced after ifd.31 deliberately: the thirty-minute recheck is worth having working in the Claude adapter before it becomes a contract other implementations inherit.

title: Recheck instead of blocking when a usage limit names no reset time
description:
yoyodyne-ifd.12 made a limit with no reset time stop the run and record a blocker, on the reasoning that a wait the harness cannot time is a guess. That was wrong about what the message means.

The operator's correction, 2026-08-16: the monthly spend message is misleading. It reports that the overage spend allowance is consumed, not that work is over. The ordinary five-hour window still resets on its usual schedule, so the run is waitable -- it simply has no reset time attached, because the value that was exhausted is not the one that governs when work resumes.

The captured payloads show the shape. A rejection carries overageStatus rejected with overageDisabledReason org_level_disabled, meaning there is no spillover capacity, while the five-hour window continues rolling: run-5b3b64b064f84f5d1c2da6bf620e6b1a shows resetsAt 1786912800 through the rejection and then 1786930800 once the window rolled, exactly eighteen thousand seconds later.

So the correct behavior when no reset time is given is to wait a bounded interval and ask again, not to give up. The operator's instruction is thirty minutes.
design:
Treat an absent reset time as unknown rather than as absent capacity. The run waits a default interval, thirty minutes, and reattempts; a reattempt that is refused again waits again. This replaces the blocker for that case only -- a reset time that is present but unparseable or in the past is still a malformed report and should not be trusted into a guessed wait.

The existing total bound is what keeps this safe and must apply to the polled case: execution.usage_limit_max_pause already bounds what one run may spend waiting in aggregate, so an account that keeps refusing walks into that bound rather than polling forever. Make the interval configurable rather than fixing thirty minutes in code.

Record each attempt so the operator can see a run is polling rather than stalled, and so the total spent waiting stays accurate.

Correct the documentation as part of this: README.md currently states that a limit with no reset time stops the run and records a blocker.
acceptance_criteria: A usage limit reported without a reset time causes the run to wait a configurable interval, defaulting to thirty minutes, and reattempt, rather than recording a blocker; repeated refusals continue to wait and reattempt; the aggregate pause bound still applies and stops a run that exceeds it; a reset time that is present but unparseable or already past is still refused rather than guessed; each wait and reattempt is recorded; README.md no longer says a missing reset time blocks the run.
notes: From the operator, 2026-08-16, correcting the reading in ifd.12: 'the monthly spend cap message is misleading. It just means that the cap for spend on overages is consumed, the regular 5 hour window cap will still reset on the same schedule. But since it doesn't return a resetsAt value, we should check again every 30 minutes.'

title: Detect a stalled provider instead of killing a working one on a wall clock
description:
A provider run is bounded by a flat thirty-minute wall clock: internal/backend/claudecode sets defaultTimeout and internal/execution wraps the process in a context.WithTimeout, so context.DeadlineExceeded becomes ProcessTimedOut. Nothing asks whether the process is still working. There is no idle, liveness, or activity check anywhere in internal/execution or the Claude Code backend.

The harness already has the signal it is not using. It parses a normalized event stream and stamps every event with a time and sequence, so it knows exactly when the last one arrived. A developer that emitted a tool result seconds ago is demonstrably not hung, whatever the elapsed total.

Observed on run-a16b7d20fc58fbb52350ca37b55a4f0b for yoyodyne-ifd.22. Events run from 19:09:04 to 19:39:03, and the final three are a Bash tool call completing without error followed by thinking tokens. It was mid-work and was killed at the wall clock. The whole run was lost: 259 insertions and a new file, nothing integrable, the full cost spent. The failure is also reported as 'developer reported failure: timed_out', which is misleading -- the developer reported nothing, the harness stopped it.
design:
Separate the two questions the single timeout is currently conflating. Whether a run is stalled is answered by activity: no events for some interval means nothing is happening, and that interval can be far shorter than thirty minutes because a working agent emits events continuously. Whether a run is worth continuing is a different question, answered by a total budget, because an agent can be live and unproductive -- retrying, looping, thrashing -- and liveness alone will never catch that. Keep both, but stop using the second to answer the first.

Losing everything is the larger defect and is worth fixing even if the thresholds stay as they are. The harness already resumes provider sessions and already returns work to the same developer inside its repair loop. A run stopped for time is closer to one paused for a usage limit than to one that failed: the worktree, branch, claimed item, and session are all still good. Ending it as resumable, rather than failed, would have cost this attempt a continuation instead of a re-run.

Consider asking before killing. A developer told its remaining time is short can finish what it is holding and summarize; a developer killed mid-edit cannot. That is only worth doing if the harness can tell a wrap-up from a stall, which is the same activity signal.

Scope the change to provider runs. The same Timeout field bounds short git commands where a flat deadline is exactly right.
acceptance_criteria: A provider run that is still emitting events is not stopped for elapsed time alone; a run that stops emitting events is detected within an interval much shorter than the current total timeout; a total budget still bounds a live but unproductive run; a run stopped for either reason preserves its worktree, branch, claimed item, and session and is reported as resumable rather than failed where the work is still good; the reported reason distinguishes a stall from an exhausted budget, and neither is described as the developer having reported a failure; git commands keep their existing flat deadlines.
notes:
Raised by the operator, 2026-08-16: 'Why would the harness kill it? Shouldn't it just check to see if the process is still going?' The answer is that it should, and it already has the event stream to do it with.

title: Publish work through pull requests, opened by the developer step and merged by the reviewer's verdict
description:
Integration currently ends at the local target branch. Nothing in the harness pushes -- there is no git push anywhere in internal/ -- and nothing opens a pull request, so main accumulates work that is invisible until the operator pushes by hand. The design document does not cover this at all: it describes a local, single-operator harness and the words push, remote branch, and pull request do not appear in it.

The operator's direction, 2026-08-16: the harness should open pull requests; the developer step is responsible for opening and pushing them; the reviewer merges them once satisfied.
design:
The harness performs, the roles decide. This is the existing rule rather than a new one -- the ownership table already gives workflow state, worktrees, checks, and integration to the harness, with agents able to request actions but not bypass policy, and the design states agents do not create, assign, merge, or remove their own worktrees. Applying it here: the developer's phase is what causes a branch to be pushed and a pull request opened, and the reviewer's approving verdict is what causes the merge, but the harness executes both. No agent is handed a credential or a shell to run gh with.

That distinction is the safety property and must not be implemented away. A reviewer agent that could merge is a reviewer that can be talked into merging; a reviewer whose verdict the harness acts on cannot bypass the checks, the independence evidence, or the fast-forward rule that already gate integration. Everything that gates integration today gates the merge.

Decide what merging means for the local target branch. Today integration fast-forwards main directly; if a pull request is the unit of promotion, the local branch either follows the merge or stops being the thing that moves, and having both would give a project two answers about where its work is.

Publishing has a wider blast radius than moving a local branch, so it belongs under approvals beside integration rather than being unconditional: a project should opt into pushing the way it opts into automatic integration, and a repository with no remote configured must degrade to today's local behavior rather than failing.

The design document's Git model needs extending as part of this, not after it.

title: Show a conversation working, and separate who said what with colour
description:
An interactive turn prints nothing between the operator's message and the reply, so a turn that takes a minute is indistinguishable from a hang. The operator hit this on 2026-08-16 and reasonably concluded the command was broken. It was not: conversation chat-2d493303331a06ef746e1ace4a942068 records the turn opening, seven consecutive provider rejections with exponential backoff over about thirty-six seconds (system api_retry, error unknown, max_retries 10), and only then the model generating. Every one of those events was recorded and none reached the operator. The harness already knows what is happening; this is a reporting gap.

The transcript should also make it obvious at a glance who is speaking and where one exchange ends and the next begins.

Split from yoyodyne-ifd.22, which now covers input separation alone after carrying all three concerns exceeded a run's timeout.
design:
Show that work is in progress and say something about what kind, without turning the terminal into an event log. A spinner or equivalent answers 'is it alive'; a short phrase for the phase answers 'what is it doing'. The event stream already carries the phases worth naming: the turn starting, provider retries, the model generating, and a tool or command running.

Provider retries deserve to be named rather than folded into generic waiting. A turn that is slow because the provider is refusing requests is telling the operator something about their account or the service, and it is the case most likely to look like a hang.

Do not let the indicator hide a real stall: an activity display that animates while nothing is happening is worse than silence, because it looks like progress.

Separate the operator's turn from the reply with a horizontal rule, and use colour to distinguish kinds of thing rather than to decorate. A question the product manager asks the operator should stand out, in orange, because a question that scrolls past unanswered stalls the work; proposals awaiting a decision and the harness's own command output are the other kinds worth distinguishing, since both are things the operator must act on rather than read.

Colour is an addition to the text, never the carrier of meaning: every distinction made with colour must survive being stripped. Honour NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb, suppress colour and rules when output is not a terminal, and keep both out of --json. The recorded event stream and reply text stay exactly as they are.
acceptance_criteria: An interactive turn shows continuous evidence of activity from the operator's message until the reply; the display names what is happening at least coarsely and names provider retries specifically; a turn with no provider activity for an extended period is distinguishable from one progressing; a horizontal rule separates the operator's turn from the reply; questions the product manager asks, proposals awaiting decision, and harness command output are visually distinguished, questions in orange; every distinction survives colour being stripped; NO_COLOR, TERM=dumb, and non-terminal output suppress colour and rules; none of it contaminates the recorded reply, the event stream, or --json.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16, in two parts: chats should provide a status indicator such as a spinner and feedback about what it is doing, so it is clear something is happening; and use colour, with questions in orange, and a horizontal rule between the operator's turn and the reply. Depends on ifd.22: an indicator that animates into the line the operator is typing makes the original complaint worse.

title: Give the product manager real authority over the tracker
description:
The product manager owns product intent but cannot act on the tracker or see enough of it to reason. Both limits are deliberate and both are wrong as they stand.

It has no tools at all: internal/chat sets AllowedTools to empty with permission mode plan, so every tracker change is dictated to the operator to type. Asked to remove a dependency, it answers that the edit is theirs. The reasoning for toollessness was that the product manager reads untrusted repository content while talking directly to the operator, so filesystem and command access is an injection surface. That holds for shell and filesystem. It does not justify blocking structured tracker operations, and conflating 'no arbitrary tools' with 'no authority' is the mistake.

It also sees very little. The briefing lists open items as titles only, capped at fifteen per group and one hundred and twenty bytes each (maxSurveyItems, maxSurveyTitleBytes in internal/chat/work.go). It cannot read a description, so it cannot tell whether proposed work belongs inside an existing item or beside it, and says so rather than guessing. Asking it to own a backlog while showing it truncated titles is asking for judgement without evidence.
design:
Grant authority through a narrow, structured tracker capability rather than by handing over general tools. Creating, updating, reparenting, reprioritising, linking and unlinking dependencies, and closing are bounded operations with named arguments that can be validated, recorded, and reversed. Shell and filesystem access remain refused, and the distinction is the point: the injection surface that argued against tools is arbitrary execution, not a typed call against the work tracker.

Goals are the exception the operator named and they stay guarded. The product manager may propose a change to a goal and may not make one, which is the existing ownership rule rather than a new restriction; what changes is that everything else stops being treated as if it were a goal.

Visibility has to match the authority. Reading an item in full is a request the product manager makes when it needs one, not a larger dump in every briefing: the survey stays a summary and detail is fetched on demand, so the context cost lands only where judgement actually requires it. The fifteen-item and one-hundred-and-twenty-byte caps are summary bounds and should stay bounds, but an item the product manager cannot read at all is worse than one it reads late.

Everything it does is recorded in the conversation and visible to the operator, and it says what it did rather than only what it decided. Treat retrieved item text as evidence, exactly as repository documents already are: a description is data describing work, never an instruction to follow.
acceptance_criteria: The product manager can create, update, reparent, reprioritise, link, unlink, and close work items directly, without dictating the change to the operator; it can read any work item in full on request rather than only titles; it still cannot change a goal, and proposes one instead; it has no filesystem, command, or network access; every tracker action it takes is recorded in the conversation and reported to the operator; retrieved work-item text is treated as evidence rather than instruction; an action that fails is reported as failed rather than described as done.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16, after a conversation in which the product manager dictated Beads edits and could not tell whether proposed work duplicated an existing item: 'The PM should have broad authority to see and edit beads -- it should only be very careful about editing goals.'

Supersedes the advisory-only stance from ifd.4.5, which was a deliberate first step rather than a permanent position. This should land before ifd.18 and ifd.24, which both assume a product manager that can actually manage a queue.

title: See and control work the harness is running on its own
description:
Once a development manager pulls from the product manager's queue and work runs without the operator starting each item, the operator needs to see what is happening and be able to stop it. Visibility is what makes autonomy acceptable rather than alarming: work proceeding out of sight is indistinguishable from work happening behind your back.

What exists today assumes the operator started the run. /status reports in flight, claimed, blocked, available, and done, and /stop cancels the run this conversation started and settles what it left behind. Neither was built for several items moving at once, chosen by something other than the operator, and /stop in particular is scoped to the conversation's own run.
design:
The operator should be able to answer three questions without leaving the conversation: what is running now and why it was chosen, what it is doing, and what it has changed. Why it was chosen is the one with no equivalent today and it is the one that matters when the harness picked the work rather than the operator: an item running with no visible reason is the failure this is meant to prevent.

Control has to reach further than one run. Stopping the item that is running, stopping a development manager from starting anything more, and stopping everything are different intentions and should not collapse into one verb. Pausing intake while letting current work finish is the case an operator reaches for when something looks wrong but not urgent, and it is the hardest to add later.

Stopping stays as careful as it is now: the existing stop settles what the cancelled run left behind rather than abandoning it, and that must hold when the stop was not aimed at a run the conversation started. Report what actually happened rather than what was asked for, including a run that finished before the stop reached it.
acceptance_criteria: The operator can see every item in flight, what each is doing, and why it was selected, without leaving the conversation; can stop one item, pause a development manager from starting more, and stop everything, as distinct actions; stopping settles what a cancelled run left behind exactly as it does today; the report says what happened rather than what was requested, including work that finished before the stop arrived; none of it requires the operator to have started the work.
notes: From the operator, 2026-08-16: 'I want visibility into how the dev managers are working and the ability to stop things.' Paired with ifd.25, which removes per-item approval: that trade is only safe if the operator can see and stop what was admitted without asking.

title: Move approval from each work item up to the goals
description:
The operator should approve goals, not every work item. Approving each item is what makes the current loop require an operator for every step, and it is the thing standing between the harness and running work on its own.

This is a return to the stated design rather than a departure from it. docs/v1-harness-design.md already says the human explicitly approves the initial brief and goals, and that lower-level approval gates are configurable but disabled by default. Per-proposal approval exists because there is no development manager yet: with nothing to decompose an approved goal into work, the product manager proposes items directly and the operator is the only thing standing between a proposal and the tracker.

Once goals are approved artifacts (yoyodyne-ifd.20) and something pulls from a product-manager-owned queue (yoyodyne-ifd.18, yoyodyne-ifd.4), the gate belongs at the goal: approve what the product should do, then watch it happen.
design:
Approval moves up a level; it does not disappear. What the operator approves is a goal, and work that traces to an approved goal is admitted without a further prompt. That places the whole weight of the arrangement on traceability actually being enforced rather than asserted, which is why this depends on yoyodyne-ifd.24: if work can reach the queue without demonstrably serving an approved goal, moving the gate up removes the gate.

Some things must still stop and ask, and they are exactly the cases the product manager is meant to escalate: work that traces to no goal, work that contradicts one, and a change to the goals themselves. A goal is amended by the operator, never by work flowing through the queue.

Keep it configurable rather than replacing one fixed policy with another. approvals already carries brief, goals, designs, and integration; per-item approval should become a policy an operator can turn back on, since the level of trust that suits an established product does not suit its first week.

The operator must be able to see what was admitted without being asked. Autonomy that is invisible is indistinguishable from work happening behind your back, so this is only safe alongside the visibility yoyodyne-ifd.26 covers.
acceptance_criteria: Work that traces to an approved goal is admitted to the queue without per-item approval; work that traces to no goal, contradicts one, or would change a goal still stops and asks; per-item approval remains available as configuration; what was admitted without asking is visible to the operator after the fact; the default for a new project is stated deliberately rather than inherited by accident.
notes:
Operator decision, 2026-08-16, asked directly before any of this was built: approval moves to the goal level as designed. The operator approves the brief and the goals; work that traces to an approved goal is admitted without a further prompt; work that traces to nothing, contradicts a goal, or would change a goal still stops and asks. Per-item approval remains available as configuration.

The operator was told plainly that this means the harness can create and run work they never individually approved, and chose it knowing that. The alternatives declined were admitting work freely but holding execution for a go-ahead, and deferring the decision until the product manager's judgement had been watched in practice.

That makes the dependencies load-bearing rather than tidy: this is only safe because ifd.24 enforces traceability rather than asserting it, ifd.18 gives the work somewhere ordered to go, and ifd.26 lets the operator see and stop what was admitted without being asked. Do not land this ahead of them.

title: Have the product manager validate proposals against its goals and say when something smells wrong
description:
The product manager should check work against its goals before proposing it, not after, and should be willing to push back rather than only comply.

Nothing checks this today. Proposal.Validate in internal/chat/proposal.go checks shape only: a title that is present, one line, and bounded; description and rationale present; parent and dependency identifiers well-formed and not duplicated. It never asks whether the proposed work serves a goal. Identifiers are only format-checked, so a proposal can name a parent that does not exist and still validate.

What holds the line today is instruction. The persona says every piece of downstream work must trace to an active goal, and the model has been observed honouring it unprompted -- declining to parent an item under the v1 epic because the work did not trace to an active goal. That is the model being conscientious, not the harness refusing.
design:
Validation runs before the operator is asked, so what reaches them is work the product manager already believes serves a goal, with the goal it serves named. A proposal that traces to nothing is not silently dropped: the product manager says it cannot place the work and asks, because unattributable work is usually a sign the goals are incomplete rather than that the request was wrong.

Being opinionated is the substantive half and needs to survive contact with a model that wants to be agreeable. When work would violate a goal, or fits the letter while cutting against the spirit of the product, the product manager says so and asks for instructions rather than proposing it with a caveat attached. The failure to design against is a concern raised so softly it reads as assent. A concern is a question that stops and waits, not a sentence in a paragraph the operator skims.

Distinguish the cases rather than collapsing them: work that serves a goal, work that serves none, work that contradicts one, and work that is technically consistent but that the product manager judges to be against the product's intent. The last is a judgement it should be willing to make and be wrong about, because an operator can overrule a stated opinion and cannot overrule one that was never voiced.

Verify what identifiers name. A parent or dependency that does not exist should fail before the operator is asked to approve it.
acceptance_criteria: Every proposal names the goal it serves, and one that traces to no goal is raised as a question rather than proposed or dropped; a proposal that would violate a goal is not proposed, and the conflict is put to the operator as a question that waits for an answer; the product manager states an opinion when work is consistent with the goals but against the product's intent; parents and dependencies are verified to exist before the operator is asked; the distinction between these cases is visible to the operator rather than flattened into one warning.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: the product manager should validate everything it proposes against its goals before proposing them, and be opinionated -- if something seems like it might violate goals or the spirit of the product, say so and request instructions.

Operator decision, 2026-08-16: approval is moving to the goal level (ifd.25), which makes this item the thing that keeps that safe. Traceability here has to be enforced rather than asserted -- if work can reach the queue without demonstrably serving an approved goal, moving the gate up removes the gate rather than raising it.

title: Separate the conversation's input from its output
description:
What the operator is typing and what the harness is writing share one stream. internal/chat reads stdin with a line-oriented bufio.Scanner and writes with plain fmt.Fprint, so anything arriving while the operator types lands in the middle of the line they are composing, and the transcript stops showing who said what or where the conversation has got to.

This is the foundation the rest of the conversation's usability rests on, which is why it is now its own item. A first attempt (run-a16b7d20fc58fbb52350ca37b55a4f0b, preserved at branch yoyodyne/yoyodyne-ifd-22/a16b7d20, commit c08f40c) carried this together with an activity indicator and colour, reached 259 insertions and a new internal/chat/display.go, and hit the thirty minute provider timeout unfinished. The indicator and colour are now yoyodyne-ifd.28 and depend on this.

It also explains a workaround already shipped. A finished background run is reported only when the operator next presses enter, asks for /status, or waits for it -- deliberately, because there is no safe moment to write unprompted. Once input has its own region that deferral can be dropped and a run can report when it actually finishes.
design:
The composing line must survive anything printed above it: a reply, a proposal, a run completing. Text already typed is never lost, reordered, or mixed with output, and the operator can tell at a glance which text is theirs and which is the product manager's.

Preserve ordinary terminal expectations while doing it -- scrollback of the conversation so far, the terminal's own copy and paste, and resizing -- since a conversation the operator cannot scroll back through or copy out of is a poor trade for a tidy input line.

Degrade honestly: when output is not a terminal this is an ordinary stream of text with no cursor control, and the recorded conversation is identical either way.
acceptance_criteria: The operator's input occupies its own region that output never writes into, so text being typed is never interrupted, reordered, or lost when a reply, a proposal, or a completing run arrives; a background run reports when it finishes rather than waiting for the operator to press a key; scrollback, copy and paste, and terminal resizing continue to work; when output is not a terminal there is no cursor control and the recorded conversation is identical; none of it reaches the recorded reply, the event stream, or --json output.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16, in three parts. First, after ./bin/yoyo chat --new appeared to do nothing: chats with the product manager should provide a status indicator such as a spinner and some feedback about what it is doing; it should be clear that something is happening. Second: use colour, with questions in orange, and a horizontal rule between the operator's turn and the product manager's reply. Third: split the input area from the output, as Claude Code does -- 'sometimes I'm typing something when a response comes back, it goes into the middle of my text and then it's not clear what the agent said and what I was typing or even where we are in the conversation.'

Sizing note for whoever picks this up: the third part changes how the conversation loop talks to the terminal, since internal/chat currently reads with a line-oriented bufio.Scanner and writes with plain fmt.Fprint. It is a larger change than the first two and they depend on it -- an activity indicator that animates into the line the operator is typing makes the reported problem worse. If this is split, build input separation first and treat the indicator, colour, and rules as what follows.

title: Have the product manager work from a configurable specifications directory
description:
The product manager should build its picture of product intent from specification documents in one configured directory, defaulting to docs/specs, rather than from whatever Markdown the repository happens to contain.

A specification opens with an introductory paragraph stating what the thing is and why it exists, followed by the goals that serve it. The goals must support and stay consistent with that introduction, and the product manager is responsible for keeping all work consistent with those goals.

Today internal/chat assembles the product manager's context from README.md, everything under docs/, and Beads state. That is broad and undirected: it mixes product intent with architecture and operator documentation, and it is why a stale sentence in README.md was reported to the operator as current product fact on 2026-08-16.
design:
Add the specifications path to the configuration schema with docs/specs as the default, resolved like other project paths and confined to the repository. It is a directory of specifications rather than one file, so the product manager holds several coherent units of intent rather than a single brief.

The structure is the contract: introduction first, goals after, goals consistent with the introduction. State it where it is enforceable rather than only in prose, and decide what the harness does with a specification that does not follow it -- refusing to load it silently loses intent, so it should surface rather than disappear.

Narrowing the product manager's inputs is a deliberate trade and should be made knowingly. Reading all of docs/ is what let it notice a contradiction between documentation and reality; reading only docs/specs makes it authoritative about intent and blind to everything else. Decide explicitly whether it still sees anything outside the specifications directory, and record the reasoning either way.

This substantially defines the product-artifact half of yoyodyne-ifd.1, which described artifact governance without settling what a product artifact looks like on disk.
acceptance_criteria: The specifications directory is configurable with docs/specs as the default and is confined to the repository; the product manager's context is built from specifications in that directory; a specification that does not follow the introduction-then-goals structure is surfaced rather than silently ignored; what the product manager can see outside the directory is a recorded decision rather than an accident; docs/configuration.md documents the setting.
notes:
Operator decision, 2026-08-16: the path is docs/product/, not docs/specs. The product manager proposed it during a conversation and the operator confirmed it when asked directly, before the path became configurable. ifd.20.1 built it and ifd.20.2 targets docs/product/goals/.

title: Collect agent findings and warnings for the operator
description:
Every agent type needs a way to report something important that does not stop its work, so it reaches the operator instead of being lost.

Today an agent can only reach the operator by failing. The pipeline records a blocker when a repair budget is spent (blockOnUnresolvedFindings, blockOnFailingCheck) and Beads has a human-needed flag, but both are terminal: they mean work stopped. Anything an agent notices while succeeding -- a risk it worked around, a fragile assumption, a discovery outside its scope -- survives only as prose in a run summary copied into bead notes, where nothing surfaces it. Real examples from this session that reached the operator only because a human was reading: the reviewer's observation that the built-in bundle's declared version had become inert, and a developer's report that bd lint could not run in its sandbox.

Collect these raw for now. Filtering by an agent is a later question and should not gate collection.
design:
A report is not a blocker and must not be modelled as one: work continues, and nothing about it stops or claims the operator's attention as a failure does. Keep the record structured enough to be filtered later without deciding the filter now -- reporting agent and role, run and work item, severity, and the text -- since a raw pile with no structure cannot be triaged when volume grows.

Every role reports through one mechanism, including the product manager, whose conversation is otherwise the only channel that reaches the operator at all. Surfacing belongs in the operator's normal path rather than a separate tool, which after ifd.16 means the product-manager conversation.

Volume is the risk. A channel that fills with routine observations gets ignored, and then it is worse than nothing because it looks like coverage. Guidance on what merits a report belongs in the role contracts, where it cannot be weakened by a persona.
acceptance_criteria: Any agent type can record a finding or warning without failing or blocking its work; reports are durable, attributed to the reporting role, run, and work item, and carry a severity; the operator can review collected reports, and after ifd.16 can do so from the product-manager conversation; a report never changes the outcome of the run that produced it; role contracts state what merits one.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: all agent types should have a mechanism to report important findings and warnings up the chain so they can be surfaced; an agent that filters them may come later, but for now collect them raw. Gated behind ifd.16.

title: Give the product manager ownership of the work backlog
description:
The product manager owns the backlog that development managers pull from. It decides what is worth doing and in what order, as the expression of product intent it already owns; a development manager takes from that ordered backlog and decomposes, sequences, and assigns the implementation work.

This makes explicit a boundary the roles already imply. The product manager owns the brief and goals but has no say today over what is actually worked on next, which means priority is set by whoever picks the next item -- currently the operator, by hand.
design:
Keep the existing ownership split rather than widening the product manager's authority into implementation. Ordering and admission to the backlog are product decisions; decomposition, dependency structure, and assignment remain the development manager's. A development manager that disagrees with an ordering proposes a change rather than reordering, exactly as downstream roles already propose changes to goals.

Priority already exists in Beads, so the question is who is authoritative for it and how that is enforced, not where to store it. Deletion is the sharp edge: removing work from a backlog can silently drop scope the operator asked for, which the product-manager persona already forbids. Retirement should be explicit and recorded, not a delete.
acceptance_criteria: The product manager can admit work to the backlog and order it, and that ordering is what a development manager consumes; a role other than the product manager cannot reorder or admit work, only propose; retiring work is explicit and recorded rather than a silent removal; the ordering is visible to the operator from the product-manager conversation.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: the product manager should be responsible for managing the backlog of work that the development manager(s) pull from. Clarified the same day: this is a priority queue, and the operator does not want to start each item by hand -- 'I don't want to have to do /work ITEMID for each thing to get it going.'

That makes this the hinge of the autonomous loop rather than a bookkeeping feature. The queue is what a development manager pulls from without being told, so ordering is not advisory: it decides what happens next. Related: ifd.24 (work is validated against goals before it reaches the queue), ifd.25 (approval moves from each item up to the goals), ifd.26 (the operator can see and stop what is pulled), ifd.3 (the scheduler that actually runs it), ifd.4 (the development manager that pulls).

title: Give the architect ownership of durable architectural invariants
description:
Architectural invariants are cross-cutting constraints that must hold across work items: a contract one item established that later items must not break. They should be rare and consequential, created, amended, and retired by the architect, and they exist to stop a developer whose own work looks correct from breaking something outside its scope.

This is currently done by hand and the absence is measurable. The first yoyodyne-ifd.2.7 attempt bypassed Store.Reserve, which was the only thing preventing two processes acting on one in-flight item. The first yoyodyne-ifd.2.8 attempt added a second resume path beside the one ifd.2.7 had just built and broke its contract, discarding 474 insertions of otherwise working code. Both were caught late by a reviewer or by failing tests, and both were prevented on the retry only because the constraint was transcribed into the bead by hand.
design:
An invariant is a durable artifact the architect owns, not prose in a bead. It needs stable identity, a statement of what must hold and why, the work item or design that established it, and a lifecycle including retirement, since an invariant that no longer holds is worse than none. Ownership follows the existing model: only the architect creates or amends one, others propose.

The point of failure to design against is delivery, not authorship. An invariant nobody puts in front of the developer does not constrain anything, so invariants relevant to a work item must reach the developer's context and the reviewer's evidence without depending on whoever wrote the bead remembering. Scope selection matters: every invariant in every prompt is both expensive and ignorable.

Relates to ifd.11, which put documentation reconciliation in the developer contract and asked the reviewer to report contradicted documentation; invariants are the same delivery problem for a stricter class of claim. Relates to ifd.2.6, which catches after the fact what invariants aim to prevent up front.
acceptance_criteria: The architect can create, amend, and retire an invariant as a durable artifact with stable identity and rationale; invariants relevant to a work item reach both the developer's context and the reviewer's evidence without per-bead transcription; a change that violates a delivered invariant draws a finding; no role other than the architect can create or amend one; retirement is explicit and recorded.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16: invariants should be rare but important, and exist to keep developers from doing work that breaks something cross-cutting or outside the scope of that developer's work. Gated behind ifd.16.

title: Threshold: manage work end to end through the product-manager conversation
description:
A threshold rather than a feature, in the style of the self-hosting thresholds in docs/v1-harness-design.md. It is met when the operator can run the product loop entirely by talking to the product manager: state intent, have it become approved goals and Beads work, see what is in flight and what is blocked, redirect or stop work, and answer what the product manager escalates -- without reaching for yoyodyne run or bd to make any of it happen.

Explicit-ID execution and direct bd access remain available for inspection, recovery, and override. The threshold is that they are no longer required for ordinary work.

Operator directive (2026-08-16): no work gated behind this threshold begins before it is met. The point is to avoid building more agent machinery that can only be driven by hand.
design: Compose what exists rather than adding a parallel path: yoyodyne chat (ifd.4.4) already holds a durable conversation, and ifd.4.5 gives the product manager a governed way to propose Beads work for operator approval. What remains is the operator seeing and steering work from inside that conversation rather than from a second tool.
acceptance_criteria: An operator can take a stated intent through to integrated work using only the product-manager conversation; can see in-flight, blocked, and completed work from within it; and can redirect or stop work through it. Nothing gated behind this threshold is started until that is demonstrated.

title: Return failing checks to the developer like reviewer findings
description:
The repair loop returns reviewer findings to the same developer for a bounded number of attempts, but a failing deterministic check ends the run outright. In internal/orchestrator/pipeline.go, activeRun.verify is called before review and again inside repairLoop after each repair attempt, and in both places a failure is returned as an error rather than handed back to the developer.

This is a real cost, not a theoretical asymmetry. Run run-b0414b72946f17eb3eb95acd5287b67f on yoyodyne-ifd.2.8 produced 474 insertions of working reconciliation code and was discarded because one test failed: the resume path it added broke TestPipelineResumesTheRepairLoopAtTheRecordedAttempt, an existing test encoding the repair-loop semantics from yoyodyne-ifd.2.7. A single iteration would very likely have fixed it. Instead the whole run was lost, and re-running costs roughly the same as the original attempt.

A failing check is better repair input than a reviewer finding: it is deterministic, reproducible, and names the exact failure.
design:
Treat a failed check as a repair trigger with the same shape and the same budget as a repair verdict. The developer is resumed in the same worktree with its session, given the failing command, its exit code, and its captured output, and the checks are then re-run.

Do not weaken the gate. The existing rule that review and integration are reachable only through passing checks must hold exactly as it does now; this changes how many times the developer may attempt to reach that state, not whether it is required. An approval must still belong to a change whose checks passed.

Decide and state whether check repairs and review repairs share one budget or hold separate ones. Sharing one is simpler and bounds total developer invocations, which is what the budget exists to do; separate budgets risk a run that alternates between the two and consumes far more than the operator expects. Record the attempts durably as the existing loop does, so an interrupted attempt still counts and a restart cannot buy a fresh budget.

Bound the failure output handed back so a verbose failing suite cannot dominate the developer's context.
acceptance_criteria: A failing check returns the command, exit code, and captured output to the same developer in the same worktree and re-runs the checks, up to the configured budget; review and integration remain unreachable while any check fails; the budget is enforced across both repair kinds and the chosen accounting is documented; attempts are recorded before the developer is invoked so a restart resumes at the right attempt; failure output handed to the developer is bounded; tests with a fake backend cover check-fail-then-pass, check-fail-until-budget-spent, and that a passing review cannot be reached with a failing check.
notes:
Found 2026-08-16 when ifd.2.8 was discarded for one failing test. Touches the same repairLoop as ifd.2.7, so it should not run concurrently with other pipeline work.

title: Pause and resume work when the provider reports a usage limit
description:
When the provider reports that a usage limit is exhausted and names a time at which it resets, the harness should wait until that time and continue, rather than treating the limit as a failure of the work.

Today it cannot even see the reset time. The Claude Code adapter's stream parser routes rate_limit_event to the outer default branch (internal/backend/claudecode/parser.go, the default in parseLine), which emits only provider_type and provider_subtype; streamEnvelope declares no field for a reset timestamp, so encoding/json discards it. Twenty rate_limit_event entries appear across recorded runs and every one has an empty payload. The transient case is already handled inside the provider CLI and surfaces as the system api_retry subtype with attempt and max_retries; this bead is about the hard case, where waiting is the only remedy.

Because the fields were discarded, the exact shape of a hard-limit envelope has never been captured. Do not infer it from documentation or from this description: capture the raw envelope first and implement against what the provider actually sends.
design:
Work in two stages, and do not skip the first. Stage one: preserve the provider's rate-limit envelope rather than reducing it to two fields, so the real payload is recorded in the event stream and can be inspected. Stage two: act on it.

Distinguish the two cases. A transient throttle is the provider CLI's business and already appears as api_retry; the harness should not duplicate that. A hard usage limit with a reset time is the harness's business, because only it knows the work is worth resuming.

On a hard limit the run must pause, not fail. Nothing is cleaned up, the Beads item stays claimed, the worktree and branch survive, and the developer session identifier is retained so work resumes in context rather than restarting. Record the reset deadline in durable run state before waiting, so a process that dies during the wait does not lose the deadline and a restart does not immediately retry into the same limit. This is the same resumability yoyodyne-ifd.2.8 builds for interrupted runs and should reuse it rather than inventing a parallel path.

Bound the wait with configuration: a maximum pause, after which the run stops and records a blocker rather than sleeping indefinitely. Treat a reset time that is absent, unparseable, or implausibly far in the future as no reset time at all and stop rather than guessing. Never busy-wait or retry before the deadline.

Open design question for the implementer to settle and state: whether a long wait should be spent in process or whether the run should exit resumable and be continued by a later invocation. Waiting in process is what the operator asked for and is simplest to reason about; an hours-long sleep in a CLI process is not. A reasonable resolution is to wait in process below a configured threshold and exit resumable above it, provided the resumable path is genuinely exercised by yoyodyne-ifd.2.8.
acceptance_criteria: A hard usage-limit report pauses the run instead of failing it, with the worktree, branch, claimed Beads item, and developer session all preserved; the reset deadline is recorded durably before the wait begins and is honored across a process restart; work resumes automatically once the deadline passes and completes normally; a missing, unparseable, or implausible reset time stops the run with a blocker rather than a guessed wait; the configured maximum pause is enforced; a transient api_retry is not mistaken for a hard limit; the provider's rate-limit payload is preserved in the event stream rather than reduced to its type; tests with a fake backend cover pause-then-resume, restart during the wait, and the refusal cases.
notes:
Raised by the operator 2026-08-16 after observing that runs stop when tokens run out. Depends on yoyodyne-ifd.2.8 because both persist and resume interrupted run state, and building them independently would produce two resume paths.
