title: Reconcile documentation as part of definition of done
description:
Every gate in the harness is diff-scoped: checks run commands against one change, and the reviewer judges one change against its work item. Nothing compares a documented claim to reality, so a change that falsifies existing documentation integrates cleanly and the documentation stays wrong.

This is not hypothetical. README.md line 38 asserted that the harness 'does not yet commit, integrate, or close the item automatically' from the moment yoyodyne-ifd.2.4 shipped automatic integration until 2026-08-16. The reviewer that approved ifd.2.4 never saw it, because README was not in that diff. It surfaced only when the product manager, whose only evidence is repository documents and Beads state, faithfully reported the stale claim as current fact to the operator.

That failure mode matters more now than it would have before: the product manager is the operator's routine interface and has no tools with which to verify anything it reads, so a false document becomes a false answer with full confidence.
design:
Two complementary parts, in order of cost.

First, make the reviewer ask whether the change falsifies anything documented. The reviewer already receives the work item, the diff, and the check results; the addition is an explicit instruction to identify documentation the change contradicts, and a finding when it does. This catches drift at the moment it is created, which is the only cheap moment. Its limit is real and should be stated rather than papered over: the reviewer sees a diff, not the whole corpus, so it will catch a change that contradicts documentation it can see and will miss one that invalidates a claim in a file the change never touches.

Second, define done for a work item as including the documentation that describes the behavior it changes. This belongs in the developer contract rather than in each bead, so it applies without every author remembering it.

Deliberately out of scope: giving the product manager tools to verify claims itself. It is toolless on purpose -- it cannot be induced to act by anything in the untrusted documents it reads -- and granting filesystem or command access to the one agent in direct conversation with the operator trades a documentation problem for a prompt-injection surface. Fix the documents instead.

The deeper blind spot, that properties of the accumulated whole are invisible from any single diff, is shared with yoyodyne-ifd.2.6 and is not fully solved here.
acceptance_criteria: The reviewer identifies and reports documentation a change contradicts, and a change that falsifies a visible documented claim draws a finding; the developer contract states that documentation describing changed behavior is part of the work; a test demonstrates the reviewer flagging a diff that contradicts documentation included in its evidence; the known limit, that claims in untouched files are not covered, is recorded rather than implied.

title: Add the two-attempt developer repair loop
description:
Milestone 1 of docs/v1-harness-design.md calls for returning reviewer findings to the same developer for a bounded number of attempts. It was never implemented: internal/orchestrator/pipeline.go fails the run on any non-approve verdict, and execution.repair_attempts_before_replan is configured, defaulted to 2, and read by nothing. One repair verdict therefore ends the run and requires a human, which is the largest single gap between the harness and the near-autonomous operation the design now states as a goal.

Feed the reviewer's findings back to the developer and re-verify, up to the configured attempt limit, before giving up.
design:
Follow the Work Execution sequence in the design document: on repair, return the findings to the same developer for up to execution.repair_attempts_before_replan attempts (default 2); after the limit, hand control back to the development manager to replan or reassign. That role does not exist yet, so the post-limit path must instead record a durable blocker on the Beads item describing the unresolved findings, rather than silently failing.

Resume the same developer session so the retry keeps its context rather than re-deriving the change from scratch. Every attempt must re-run the deterministic checks and obtain a fresh independent review; an earlier approval must never carry over, and the existing independence evidence (distinct developer and reviewer sessions) must hold on the attempt that ultimately integrates. Preserve the worktree and branch across attempts.

Record the attempt count in durable run state so an interrupted process resumes at the right attempt and cannot exceed the limit by restarting. The reviewer's findings are the developer's input for the next attempt and should be passed as structured findings rather than prose.

TWO CONSTRAINTS FROM A REJECTED FIRST ATTEMPT (run-40b6827595434281826e793db69ac5f2, preserved for reference only at branch yoyodyne/yoyodyne-ifd-2-7/40b68275, commit 5a28d8a). Both were found by the independent reviewer and must not recur:

1. Concurrency. Any resume or retry path must acquire the same reservation that Store.Reserve provides for a fresh run. The first attempt added a resume path that bypassed it, so two concurrent invocations could both act on one in-flight item and together exceed the configured attempt limit. Reservation is the only thing preventing that; a new entry point into an in-flight run must not sidestep it.

2. Durable schema compatibility. State files written by the current binary exist on disk right now with review_findings encoded as an integer. The first attempt redefined that key as a list of structured findings and bumped StateSchemaVersion 1 to 2 with no handling for existing files, which would make every one of them fail to decode in Store.Load. If the findings must become structured, either use a new key and leave the old one readable, or handle schema 1 explicitly on load. Verify against the real files in the run state directory rather than reasoning about it. More generally, a schema bump is only complete when a file written by the previous version still loads.

Three separate functions were conflated while running Milestone 1 by hand. They belong to different roles and skipping any one of them reproduces a failure we actually hit.

1. Architect, prospective. Establishing that a contract is a contract. The repair loop (ifd.2.7) recorded attempts before invoking the developer specifically so an interrupted attempt still counts and a restart cannot buy a fresh budget. That is an invariant, not an implementation detail, and the architect persona already asks for exactly this: make invariants explicit, say which must be enforced in code, and design for the system that exists rather than placing a better mechanism inconsistently beside it. 2. Development manager, transcription. An invariant nobody writes into the work item does not reach the developer, because the developer reads the bead. The role already owns converting designs into Beads work with acceptance criteria and considering side effects and integration order. Concretely this is what carrying the two ifd.2.7 findings into its design section did, what adding the resume-path constraint to ifd.2.8 did, and what noting that ifd.13 must not run concurrently with other pipeline work did. The three durable-evidence findings on PR #3 -- target_branch shape, CleanupIntegrated coherence with its worktree, and integration evidence stored against a pre-integration phase -- were emergent from accumulated code. Nobody would have written them down in advance. Architecture prevents the foreseeable; wider-scope review detects the rest.

ARCHITECT VERSUS PRODUCT MANAGER. Ownership is enforced, not stylistic: the product manager owns the brief and goals, the architect owns designs and specifications, and neither revises the other's, they propose. The product manager answers what should be true and why, faces the operator, and is done when intent is unambiguous and specific enough to design against. The architect answers how given this system, faces developers, and is done when someone else could implement the design and a reviewer could tell from the design alone whether they did. Escalation layers accordingly: a developer proposes an upstream change, the architect evaluates it and owns the design amendment, and only an unworkable goal reaches the product manager. That buffer is what stops product intent bending to whatever was convenient to build.

Observed 2026-08-16: the product manager, told the README was stale, proposed the fixes and then said the design-document edits were the architect's to make and should go as a proposal rather than direct edits. The boundary held without being prompted.

The blur is non-functional intent. Nearly autonomous operation is a goal; that achieving it requires the repair loop and restart reconciliation is design. The design document resolves this by making it the product manager's job to state a goal specifically enough to design against.

GROUNDING CAUTION. The architect is an agent reasoning from documents, and on 2026-08-16 the product manager confidently reported a stale README as current fact because its only evidence is repository documents and Beads state. The architect inherits that exposure and is worse affected, because its output becomes binding constraints on downstream work rather than advice to a human who can push back. ifd.11, documentation reconciliation as part of definition of done, is therefore load-bearing for the architect in a way it is not for the product manager, and should land before this milestone leans on architect-authored invariants.

title: Put a price tag on every completed work item
description:
When the operator asks what is done, each completed item should come back with what it cost. The evidence already exists and is already attributed: every provider invocation ends in a run.completed event carrying the provider-reported usage and total_cost_usd, and every run records the work item it served. Nothing joins them, so cost today is answerable per run (yoyo-status -c) but not per item, and not from inside a conversation at all.

The join matters because it changes what the number means. An item's honest price includes every run it took: failed attempts, discarded first tries, and repair attempts, developer and reviewer invocations both. yoyodyne-ifd.2.7 cost roughly twenty-eight dollars across a rejected attempt and a successful one; a per-run view shows two numbers and a per-item view shows the truth.
design:
Record the cost durably on the item when a run for it completes, aggregating across all of its runs, so the tracker carries the price and everything that reads the tracker -- the product manager's briefing, /show, bd itself -- sees it without a second data source. Use the provider-reported cost, never an estimate from a price table that can drift.

Surface it where the operator actually asks. The question 'what is done' is asked in the conversation, so completed items in /status carry their price, and /show breaks it down by run: attempt, outcome, cost. yoyo-status may grow a by-item grouping, but the conversation is the primary surface.

Backfill what already happened: the durable run state and event streams for past runs still exist under the state directory, so closed items can be priced retroactively rather than starting the ledger today.

Scope honestly: runs only. Conversation turns also cost money and are recorded, but attributing a conversation that discussed five items is a judgement call this item should not attempt; note the gap rather than solving it. A run whose events are gone prices as unknown, stated as unknown rather than zero -- a zero that means 'no record' would corrupt every total it touches.
acceptance_criteria: A completed work item carries the total provider-reported cost of every run made for it, including failed and repair attempts and reviewer invocations; asking what is done in the conversation shows each item's price; /show breaks the cost down by run with outcomes; existing closed items are backfilled from recorded run state; a run with no surviving record prices as unknown, never zero; costs are provider-reported, not estimated.
notes: From the operator, 2026-08-17: 'lets us get the token cost for each completed item so that when I ask what's done they come back with a price tag.' Related: yoyo-status -c already prices runs (and excludes conversations, a known gap recorded on ifd.23); this item is the per-item join and the conversational surface.

title: Stream the reply and surface run milestones while the operator watches
description:
A turn's reply appears all at once when it completes; until then the spinner from ifd.28 says something is happening but not what is being said. And a background run started with /work is silent between prompts -- its milestones exist in the event stream but are reported only when the operator next asks.

Three parts. First, stream the product manager's reply as the provider generates it, replacing the spinner with prose forming. Second, when this conversation started a run, print one-line milestone notices as it crosses phases: checks passed, review approve, pull request queued, merged. Third, small comforts: a terminal bell and title update when a background run finishes, and per-turn cost in the status line, since the operator watches spend.
design:
Streaming is the invasive part and belongs behind the backend boundary: the Claude Code adapter already parses assistant events incrementally, so the text exists before the terminal result -- what changes is that the console shows it as it arrives rather than holding it. The recorded reply must be byte-identical to the non-streamed one, redaction must run on every fragment before it is shown, and a stream that dies mid-reply must not leave a half-reply looking whole: say plainly that it was cut off.

Milestones reuse the notices channel that already carries harness activity into the conversation, printed above the input region ifd.22 built, so they never corrupt what the operator is typing. Keep them to phase transitions -- an event log scrolling by is exactly what the activity display was designed not to be.

Bell and title are terminal escapes behind the same capability checks as colour; cost comes from the usage the provider already reports per turn. All of it degrades to nothing when output is not a terminal.
acceptance_criteria: The reply appears as it is generated and the recorded conversation is byte-identical to the non-streamed form; redaction applies to every fragment before display; an interrupted stream is reported as interrupted; a run started from the conversation reports phase transitions as they happen without corrupting input; a finished background run rings the bell and updates the title where the terminal supports it; per-turn cost appears in the status line; NO_COLOR, TERM=dumb, non-terminal output, and --json see none of it.

title: Design a portable agent configuration system
description:
TODO recorded by the operator, 2026-08-16, when choosing explicit project configuration for now: 'we will want those later ... the design for a more portable agent configuration system remains a TODO.'

The machinery exists and works. A versioned bundle ships inside the executable, a project inherits it by name with extends, three layers resolve with later ones winning, checks are replaced wholesale rather than concatenated, a persona override replaces rather than merges, and version is deliberately not inheritable. What is missing is not capability but a considered answer to what portability should mean once there is more than one project and more than one person.

ifd.35 makes the explicit file the shape a project is shipped with, precisely because the operator is changing agent properties often at this stage and wants an edit's effect obvious. Inheritance is retained rather than removed, so this is deferred rather than discarded.
design:
The question worth answering is what a project should own and what it should receive. An explicit configuration is clear and never improves; an inherited one improves and hides where its values came from. Both are right at different points in a project's life, and the interesting design is the transition between them rather than a choice of one.

Things that will need deciding when this is picked up: whether a project can inherit selectively rather than wholesale, so it owns the agent properties it edits often and inherits the rest; how an operator sees which values are inherited without running a command, given that config show --origins already answers this only when asked; how a bundle improvement reaches a project that has materialized its defaults, which is the specific thing ifd.35 trades away; and whether bundles are ever supplied by anyone other than the executable, which is where this meets ifd.32 and its plugin contract.

Do not start this by writing code. The resolution machinery is already built and tested; what is absent is the decision about when a project should use it.
acceptance_criteria: A recorded design states what a project owns versus inherits, how an operator can see which is which without asking, how a project moves between explicit and inherited configuration in both directions, and how an improvement to shared defaults reaches a project that has materialized them; the design is traceable to a goal; no code is written before that design is agreed.
notes: Deferred deliberately, not abandoned. The inheritance implementation from ifd.4.2, its tightening in ifd.9, and ifd.4.3 all remain live; ifd.35 changes the default shape a project is shipped with rather than removing what the harness can express.

title: Settle the architect and development-manager artifact homes
description:
Open design question raised by the operator on 2026-08-16, deliberately not settled: if the product manager works from specifications in docs/specs (yoyodyne-ifd.20), the architect and the development manager plausibly want the same treatment -- the architect for architectural invariants, possibly as ADRs in a directory, and the development manager for design documents. Both artifact kinds support the product manager's goals.

This is filed as a question rather than a feature because it reassigns ownership in a way the current design document contradicts, and getting that wrong is expensive to unwind.
design:
RESOLVED by the operator, 2026-08-16. The architect keeps designs and additionally owns decision records and invariants; the development manager decomposes those designs into work without owning a document of its own.

Artifact ownership after this decision:
- product manager: docs/product/ -- the brief and the goals derived from it
- architect: docs/designs/ -- designs and specifications, unchanged from what the design document already states; and a decision home for ADRs and the invariants extracted from them
- development manager: no document; it converts approved designs into Beads work with dependencies and acceptance criteria

This is deliberately the smallest change from what is written and shipped: the artifact ownership table gains a row rather than moving one, and the architect and development-manager personas need no rewrite. The alternative considered and rejected was moving designs to the development manager, which would have been a cleaner separation between system-wide constraints and how one body of work is structured, but would have rewritten the ownership table, the intent graph, and both personas for a role that does not exist yet.

ADRs and invariants remain complementary rather than alternatives, as recorded before: an ADR is the durable record of a decision, with a status that can become superseded, and an invariant is the live constraint extracted from it. Using either as the other fails predictably -- edit ADRs to stay current and the decision history rots; bury live constraints in historical prose and nothing can tell what currently holds. The architect owns both, and yoyodyne-ifd.17 is what makes an invariant reach a developer, which is the only thing that makes it constrain anything.
acceptance_criteria: The artifact ownership table and intent graph in docs/v1-harness-design.md record the decision above, adding the architect's decision and invariant home without moving designs; the architect and development-manager personas remain consistent with it; the relationship between decision records and invariants is stated rather than implied.

From the operator, 2026-08-16, phrased tentatively: 'possibly we should have a similar set up for the architect ... and the dev manager ... both of those artifacts should support the PMs goals.' Recorded as an open question rather than a decision. Relates to ifd.17 (architect owns invariants), ifd.20 (product manager specifications), and ifd.1 (artifact governance).

title: Add restart reconciliation for interrupted runs
description:
Milestone 1 calls for restart reconciliation and duplicate-run prevention. Duplicate-run prevention exists (ExistingRunError), but nothing reconciles an interrupted run. The code repeatedly documents a reconciler that does not exist: internal/orchestrator/pipeline.go describes leaving 'a succeeded run in the cleaning_up phase with worktree_removed still false, which is a resumable instruction rather than a lost run', and internal/gitworktree/manager.go documents CleanupIntegrated as resumable specifically so a reconciler can finish it.

This matters beyond tidiness: the durable-evidence invariants tightened during PR #3 review were all defensive against a reconciler reading state back, and that consumer still does not exist, so none of them are exercised.
design:
Compare durable run state against observed reality at startup, as the Recovery and Idempotency section describes: the recorded phase, the worktree registration, the branch, whether the recorded source commit is contained in the target, and provider session state where queryable. Then resume cleanup, mark an external outcome, or raise a durable blocker. Never start a second developer for an item because a process handle was lost. Cleanup over already-absent artifacts must remain a safe no-op.

CONSTRAINT FROM A FAILED FIRST ATTEMPT (run-b0414b72946f17eb3eb95acd5287b67f, preserved for reference only at branch yoyodyne/yoyodyne-ifd-2-8/b0414b72, commit ee5b231). That attempt produced working reconciliation code and was discarded because make test failed on TestPipelineResumesTheRepairLoopAtTheRecordedAttempt.

Build on the resume path that already exists rather than introducing a second one. yoyodyne-ifd.2.7 restructured the run onto activeRun and added resumption that continues the repair loop at the recorded attempt, deliberately so an interrupted attempt still counts and a restart cannot buy a fresh repair budget. Its tests encode that contract. Reconciliation must extend that path and keep those tests passing; if a test must change, the change has to be justified as a corrected contract rather than adjusted to fit new code. Run the full suite, not only new tests: the failure here was a pre-existing test in internal/orchestrator, not one this work would add.
acceptance_criteria: An interrupted run in each non-terminal phase is reconciled to a correct terminal state or an explicit blocker; a run interrupted between integration and cleanup completes its cleanup without re-running the developer; reconciliation is idempotent and safe to run repeatedly; a run whose artifacts are already gone reconciles without error; tests cover interruption at each phase boundary.

title: Verify language agnosticism with a non-Go fixture project
description:
Support for projects in languages other than Go is now a recorded goal and a design invariant (docs/v1-harness-design.md: the harness assumes no language, build system, or test framework, and verification is whatever commands the project declares). Nothing verifies it. Every fixture and every check example in the repository is Go, so the claim currently rests on the observation that internal/checks/runner.go shells out to /bin/sh -c and reads an exit code.

Add a fixture project whose configured checks are not Go commands and drive it through the harness end to end, so a future change that quietly introduces a Go assumption -- in context assembly, worktree handling, diff summarization, or check execution -- fails a test rather than surfacing when someone points Yoyodyne at a TypeScript or Python repository.
design: The harness's only contact with a toolchain is running declared commands and reading exit codes, so this needs a fixture whose checks are not Go commands, not a second language integration and not a dependency on a language runtime being installed in CI. Prefer checks that are plain shell (a script in the fixture that exits 0 or 1) over commands requiring node, python, or a JVM, so the test verifies the harness's language independence rather than the CI image's contents. Cover both a passing and a failing check, since the failing path is what gates integration.
acceptance_criteria: A fixture project with non-Go checks runs through the harness end to end; a failing non-Go check stops the run before review and integration exactly as a failing Go check does; the test requires no language runtime beyond a POSIX shell; the language-agnostic invariant in docs/v1-harness-design.md is cited by the test so the link between claim and verification is discoverable.

title: Add branch-scope review over an accumulated change
description: The independent reviewer sees exactly one work item's worktree diff (review.Request carries a single gitworktree.ChangeDiff), so it structurally cannot see defects that only appear across accumulated beads. PR #3 demonstrated this concretely: three of its five findings were cross-cutting durable-evidence invariants in internal/runstate and internal/gitworktree, each individually consistent within the bead that introduced it and only visible against the combined shape of the branch. Those were found by an external reviewer, not by the harness. Give the harness a review scope that covers an accumulated change against a base, so that class of finding is caught by the loop rather than by whoever happens to open the pull request.
design: Reuse the existing reviewer contract, structured verdict, and independence evidence; vary the change under review rather than the review protocol. The diff is a branch against a recorded base commit rather than one worktree, so the existing DiffLimits truncation and redaction paths need to hold over a much larger change, and the reviewer must be told that findings may span commits. Decide explicitly whether a branch-scope repair verdict blocks anything or is advisory, since the per-bead work it covers is already integrated by the time this runs.
acceptance_criteria: The harness can run an independent structured review over a branch against a base commit and record the verdict with the same session and model evidence as a per-item review; diff limits and redaction hold over a multi-commit change; the outcome of a repair verdict at this scope is defined and enforced; tests cover a multi-commit review with a fake backend.
notes: Raised 2026-08-15 from PR #3 review. The operator asked that the harness reviewer take over review work; this bead is what makes that true at the pull-request scope rather than only per work item.

title: Handle concurrent integration contention on a shared target branch
description: Adversarial review of PR #3 traced two runs racing to fast-forward the same target branch. Both promotion paths fail closed under contention -- the in-primary 'git merge --ff-only' hits index lock contention, and the non-checked-out path's 'update-ref' compare-and-swap loses the race on the old-value mismatch -- so no corruption or force-advance is possible. The gap is liveness, not safety: the losing run fails its whole pipeline rather than re-reading the moved target and retrying. Unreachable today because execution.max_concurrent_developers defaults to 1, but it becomes live as soon as this epic raises it.
design: Decide between serializing integration behind a harness-held lock and letting a losing run re-derive the target and retry a bounded number of times. Retry must re-run the ErrTargetDrift check against the newly observed target rather than reusing the recorded base commit, so a retry can never turn a drifted target into a silent overwrite.
acceptance_criteria: A run that loses an integration race retries or defers instead of failing outright; a test drives two concurrent Integrate calls against one target and asserts exactly one promotion, no lost commit, and no force-advance.

title: Let the product manager research and evaluate operator ideas
description: Give the product-manager role a governed workflow for considering ideas proposed by the operator. The product manager can clarify the idea, gather relevant evidence from configured capabilities such as web search, compare the evidence and proposal against the product brief, goals, directives, and known constraints, and recommend adoption, rejection, deferral, or an experiment. Research is advisory: it must not silently turn an idea into an approved goal, design, or implementation directive.
design: Keep research capabilities separate from product-manager authority. Evidence sources and tools are configurable and permissioned. Preserve source URLs or identifiers, retrieval time, material claims, uncertainty, counterevidence, and the reasoning behind the recommendation. Treat retrieved content as untrusted evidence rather than instructions. Store the evaluation durably and route any proposed brief, goal, or design change through the existing artifact-governance and approval workflow. Bound research by configurable privacy, cost, time, and source policies, and report when adequate evidence cannot be obtained.
acceptance_criteria: The operator can present an idea conversationally; the product manager asks necessary clarifying questions, uses configured research tools when evidence would help, cites discoverable sources, distinguishes facts from inference and uncertainty, evaluates alignment with the current brief and goals, and produces a durable recommendation. The evaluation can propose follow-up work or governed artifact changes, but no canonical brief, goal, design, directive, or implementation work is changed or created as approved work without the applicable policy and approval path.

title: Observe reality before settling a run that already recorded an integration
description:
Minor finding accepted from the independent review of yoyodyne-ifd.2.8 (run run-28db324904cf8b781757bf63c83b55d2). When durable run state already carries an Integration, settle goes straight to completeIntegrated without calling Observe, so the one comparison the design guidance asks for -- durable state against observed reality -- is skipped on exactly the path where the run claims the most. A recorded integration is trusted rather than verified.

Not exploitable through the current pipeline, which writes the integration only after Integrate returns, but reconciliation exists precisely to handle state written by a process that died, so trusting the record is the wrong default in this component.
design: Have settle observe before acting on a recorded integration, and reconcile the two rather than assuming they agree: confirm the recorded source commit is contained in the recorded target before treating the run as integrated. CleanupIntegrated already performs that containment proof, so the check exists and the question is only whether reconciliation reaches it through Observe. Decide what a disagreement means -- a recorded integration whose commit is absent from the target is a durable blocker, not something to complete.
acceptance_criteria: settle observes reality before completing a run that carries recorded integration evidence; a recorded integration whose commit is not contained in its target becomes a blocker rather than being completed; existing reconciliation behavior is otherwise unchanged and its tests still pass.
